{\footnotesize\tikz[baseline=-0.6ex]\draw[blue,very thick] (0,0) -- (0.7,0);\ $t\mapsto W_T^{-1}(W_T(t|\sigma_2,OC)|\sigma_1,OC)$\qquad\tikz[baseline=-0.6ex]\draw[black,thick,dashed] (0,0) -- (0.7,0);\ $45^\circ$ line\par}
% Caption kept here, deliberately not typeset - the figure carries a
% number only.  To restore it, move the line below into \caption{}.
% The QQ plots $t\mapsto W_T^{-1}(W_T(t|\sigma_2,OC)|\sigma_1,OC)$ under a convex (a) and a concave (b) mills ratio. The curve leaves the $45^{\circ}$ line from below and single crosses it at the pivotal rank $q^*$, so applicants ranked below $q^*$ gain and those above lose. $G$ standard normal. Both begin at $OC/v^T$, the winning probability of the marginal applicant, which is common to both noise levels. Only the merit distribution differs between this figure and its companion: $OC$, $\lambda^T$, $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are common. $F$ standard normal, $\sigma_1=0.4$, $\sigma_2=1.2$; $v^T=1$, $OC=0.08$, $\lambda^T=0.4$.
\caption{\footnotesize Both figures show the QQ pot of the winning probability distribution in the top program. The $y$ axis corresponds to the distribution before the rise in noise $\sigma_1$, while the $x$ axis corresponds to the distribution after the rise in noise to $\sigma_2>\sigma_1$. As we can see, higher noise involves a transfer of winning rents from the best applicants to the worst when the mills ratio is convex. The opposite is true when the mills ratio is concave.}
\label{fig:qq}
\end{figure}
